slides.assertion: How do you settle a continent — and who pays the price when you do?
In 1862, Congress offered 160 acres of free land to anyone who would farm it for five years.
The Transcontinental Railroad (1869) cut a cross-country trip from months to days — and opened the West to settlement and extraction.
Chinese laborers built much of the Central Pacific — doing the most dangerous work while facing open discrimination.
The same expansion forced relocations, broke treaties, and collapsed the buffalo herds Plains nations depended on.
slides.footer: US.01 · The Cost to Native Nations

slides.assertion: The law itself shows the government's intent — read who it includes, and who it leaves out.

sourceItFirst.why: A law reveals the government’s intent — ask who benefits and who is left out.

sources.title: Homestead Act
sources.author: U.S. Congress
sources.excerpt: Any person who is the head of a family, or who has arrived at the age of twenty-one years, and is a citizen of the United States... shall be entitled to enter one quarter section [160 acres] of unappropriated public lands.

sources.title: Pacific Railway Act
sources.author: U.S. Congress
sources.excerpt: The United States shall extinguish as rapidly as may be the Indian titles to all lands falling under the operation of this act... There is hereby granted to the said company... every alternate section of public land, designated by odd numbers.

perspectives.prompt: Who gained land, wealth, power, or protection from this event?
perspectives.us01: Settlers who claimed 160-acre homesteads; railroad companies that received alternate-section land grants; eastern markets and manufacturers reached by the new rail lines.

perspectives.prompt: Who lost land, labor, freedom, or life — and who was silenced?
perspectives.us01: Plains nations, who lost lands and treaty rights and whose buffalo herds collapsed; Chinese laborers, who did the most dangerous railroad work while facing wage discrimination and exclusion.

perspectives.prompt: Which people, offices, or courts held the authority to make the choice?
perspectives.us01: The U.S. Congress and the federal government, acting through the Homestead Act and the Pacific Railway Act of 1862.

slides.assertion: Trace one effect: the railroad → the buffalo → the people.

weDo.modeledPrompt: Trace ONE effect of the Transcontinental Railroad on American Indian nations.
weDo.modeled: CAUSE: The railroad cut directly through Plains hunting grounds (1869).  →  EFFECT: Settlers and hunters poured in and the buffalo herds collapsed.  →  CONSEQUENCE: Plains nations lost the food source their economy depended on and were pushed onto reservations.
weDo.think: Watch how I do it: I start with the policy (the cause), I underline the change it set in motion (the effect), then I push one step further to the human consequence. I do NOT stop at "railroad was built" — I ask "so what happened to people because of it?"
weDo.thenYou: Now you complete two more cause→effect chains on your own in the activity.

slides.assertion: A hometown hero: George Jordan of Triune, Williamson County — the only Medal of Honor recipient from our county.

tnFacts.claim: George Jordan was born around 1847 in the Triune area of Williamson County, Tennessee.
He is the only Medal of Honor recipient from Williamson County.
He served with the 9th U.S. Cavalry (Buffalo Soldiers), earning the Medal of Honor for Fort Tularosa (1880) and Carrizo Canyon (1881), issued in 1890.

slides.mapNote: 1878 Williamson County map (Tennessee State Library & Archives) locating Triune, Jordan's home community.

slides.title: Federal Policies Toward American Indians
slides.tnStandard: US.02 – Examine federal policies toward American Indians, including the movement to reservations, assimilation, boarding schools, and the Dawes Act.
slides.iCan: I can examine federal policies toward American Indians, including the movement to reservations, assimilation, boarding schools, and the Dawes Act.

slides.assertion: After the Civil War, the federal government confined American Indian nations to reservations far smaller than their homelands.
Boarding schools like Carlisle pursued forced assimilation under the motto “Kill the Indian, save the man.”
The Dawes Act (1887) broke up tribal land — holdings fell from 138 million acres to 48 million by 1934.
slides.footer: US.02 · The Dawes Act & Its Impact

slides.assertion: The Dawes Act itself shows the government’s intent — read what it did to communal land.

sourceItFirst.why: A law reveals intent — ask what it dismantled and who gained the “surplus” land.

perspectives.prompt: Who gained land, wealth, power, or protection?
perspectives.answer: White settlers who purchased “surplus” reservation land; railroads and speculators; the federal government advancing westward settlement.

perspectives.prompt: Who lost land, labor, freedom, or life — and who was silenced?
perspectives.answer: American Indian nations, who lost 90 million acres, communal landholding, languages, and children taken to boarding schools — a documented cultural genocide.

perspectives.prompt: Which people, offices, or courts held the authority?
perspectives.answer: The U.S. Congress and the Office of Indian Affairs, acting through the Dawes Act and reservation/assimilation policy.

slides.title: Compromise of 1877, Jim Crow & Plessy v. Ferguson
slides.tnStandard: US.03 – Explain the impact of the Compromise of 1877, including Jim Crow laws, lynching, disenfranchisement methods, the efforts of Benjamin “Pap” Singleton and the Exodusters, and the Plessy v. Ferguson decision.
slides.iCan: I can explain the impact of the Compromise of 1877, including Jim Crow laws, lynching, disenfranchisement, the Exodusters, and Plessy v. Ferguson.

slides.assertion: The Compromise of 1877 withdrew federal troops from the South — ending Reconstruction and its protections.
slides.footer: US.03 · The Election of 1876 & End of Reconstruction

slides.assertion: With protection gone, Southern states built Jim Crow — segregation, poll taxes, literacy tests, and lynching.
Pap Singleton led the Exodusters — thousands of Black Southerners who migrated to Kansas to escape Jim Crow terror.
Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) made “separate but equal” law — legitimizing segregation for nearly sixty years.
The Court’s own words show the doctrine — read what “separate but equal” actually authorized.

sourceItFirst.who: The Supreme Court of the United States (7–1 majority, Justice Brown).
sourceItFirst.why: A ruling sets the law of the land — ask what it permitted and whom it left unprotected.

sources.title: Plessy v. Ferguson (majority opinion)
sources.author: Supreme Court of the United States
sources.excerpt: Laws permitting, and even requiring, [the] separation [of the races] in places where they are liable to be brought into contact do not necessarily imply the inferiority of either race...

sources.title: Harlan dissent, Plessy v. Ferguson
sources.author: Justice John Marshall Harlan
sources.excerpt: Our Constitution is color-blind, and neither knows nor tolerates classes among citizens.

slides.assertion: Return to three questions: who benefited, who bore the costs, who decided.
slides.framingIntro: A historian returns to three questions at the end of every reading. Use them to analyze this standard.

perspectives.prompt: Who gained land, wealth, power, or protection?
perspectives.answer: White Democratic “Redeemer” governments in the South, who regained political control; the national parties that traded away Black civil rights for the presidency.

perspectives.prompt: Who lost land, labor, freedom, or life — and who was silenced?
perspectives.answer: African Americans, who lost federal protection, the vote, and equal access — and faced lynching. Those who resisted, like the Exodusters, were forced to flee.

perspectives.prompt: Which people, offices, or courts held the authority?
perspectives.answer: The disputed 1876 electoral commission and party leaders (Compromise of 1877); Southern legislatures (Jim Crow laws); and the U.S. Supreme Court (Plessy).

slides.title: Gilded Age Politics and Economics
slides.tnStandard: US.04 – Analyze the causes and consequences of Gilded Age politics and economics, including political machines, major scandals, civil service reform, and the economic differences between farmers, wage earners, and industrial capitalists.
slides.iCan: I can analyze the causes and consequences of Gilded Age politics and economics, including political machines, scandals, civil service reform, and economic inequality.

slides.assertion: Political machines like Boss Tweed’s Tammany Hall ran cities through patronage — funneling millions in public funds.
Scandals ran deep: Crédit Mobilier and the spoils system — until Garfield’s 1881 assassination forced reform.
The Pendleton Act (1883) began merit-based hiring; the Interstate Commerce Act (1887) began federal economic regulation.
Wealth concentrated at the top while farmers and wage earners struggled with debt, low pay, and danger.
A close observer named the era’s corruption — read how power actually worked in the Gilded Age.

sourceItFirst.who: James Bryce, British observer of American government.
sourceItFirst.why: An outside observer describes what insiders took for granted — ask what he says corrupted city government.

sources.title: The American Commonwealth

sources.excerpt: The Boss... has a fine sense of political values... He dispenses places, rewards the loyal, punishes the mutinous... The machine works because it feeds those who serve it.

perspectives.prompt: Who gained land, wealth, power, or protection?
perspectives.answer: Political bosses and their machines; industrial capitalists who concentrated wealth; office-seekers rewarded by the spoils system.

perspectives.prompt: Who lost land, labor, freedom, or life — and who was silenced?
perspectives.answer: Farmers facing falling prices and high rail rates; wage earners in dangerous, low-paid jobs; taxpayers whose funds were siphoned by machines.

perspectives.prompt: Which people, offices, or courts held the authority?
perspectives.answer: City machines and party bosses; the U.S. Congress, which passed the Pendleton Act (1883) and Interstate Commerce Act (1887).

slides.title: Inventions & Innovations of Business Leaders & Entrepreneurs
slides.tnStandard: US.05 – Describe the changes in American life that resulted from the inventions and innovations of business leaders and entrepreneurs of the period, including Bell, Bessemer, Carnegie, Edison, Morgan, Rockefeller, Tesla, Vanderbilt, Madam C.J. Walker, and George Washington Carver.
slides.iCan: I can describe the changes in American life that resulted from the inventions and innovations of business leaders and entrepreneurs of the period.

slides.assertion: New inventions reshaped daily life: Bell’s telephone, Edison’s light and power, Tesla’s AC, Bessemer’s steel.
Industrial titans consolidated power: Carnegie (steel), Rockefeller (oil), Morgan (finance), Vanderbilt (rail).
African American entrepreneurs broke through: Madam C.J. Walker built a fortune; Carver transformed Southern farming.
Carnegie explained how the rich should use their wealth — read his “Gospel of Wealth.”

sourceItFirst.why: A titan justifies his own fortune — ask what he claims the wealthy owe society, and what he leaves out about workers.

sources.excerpt: The man who dies thus rich dies disgraced... This, then, is held to be the duty of the man of wealth: to consider all surplus revenues... as trust funds... to produce the most beneficial results for the community.

sources.title: The Freeman (on Madam C.J. Walker)
sources.author: The Freeman (Indianapolis)

perspectives.prompt: Who gained land, wealth, power, or protection?
perspectives.answer: Industrialists who amassed fortunes; consumers gaining new technologies; entrepreneurs like Walker and Carver who created jobs and products.

perspectives.prompt: Who lost land, labor, freedom, or life — and who was silenced?
perspectives.answer: Workers who faced dangerous conditions and low wages while owners consolidated monopolies; small competitors bought out or driven under.

perspectives.prompt: Which people, offices, or courts held the authority?
perspectives.answer: Private business leaders — Carnegie, Rockefeller, Morgan, Vanderbilt — and the inventors and entrepreneurs whose choices reshaped the economy.

slides.title: Industrial Centers and Urbanization
slides.tnStandard: US.06 – Locate major industrial centers, and describe how industrialization influenced the movement of people from rural to urban areas: Boston, Chicago, New York City, Pittsburgh, San Francisco.
slides.iCan: I can locate major industrial centers and describe how industrialization moved people from rural to urban areas.

slides.assertion: Industry clustered by geography: Pittsburgh steel, Chicago rail & meatpacking, NYC finance, Boston textiles, San Francisco Pacific trade.
Factory wages pulled millions off farms — Chicago grew from 30,000 in 1850 to over 1 million by 1890.
Cities grew faster than they could cope — crowded tenements, poor sanitation, and new social problems.
A map is a primary source too — read where manufacturing wage earners concentrated in 1890.

sourceItFirst.why: A statistical map shows where industry pulled people — ask which regions drew workers and which were left behind.

perspectives.prompt: Who gained land, wealth, power, or protection?
perspectives.answer: Factory owners with a concentrated labor supply; cities that grew into commercial powers; workers who found steady wages.

perspectives.prompt: Who lost land, labor, freedom, or life — and who was silenced?

slides.title: Immigration: Old vs. New Immigrants
slides.tnStandard: US.07 – Describe the differences between “old” and “new” immigrants, analyze the assimilation process, and determine the impacts of increased migration on American society, including Ellis Island, Angel Island, push/pull factors, nativism, the Chinese Exclusion Act, and the Gentlemen’s Agreement.
slides.iCan: I can describe the differences between “old” and “new” immigrants, analyze assimilation, and determine the impacts of increased migration on American society.

slides.assertion: “Old” immigrants came from Northern/Western Europe; “new” immigrants (1880–1920) came from Southern/Eastern Europe and Asia.
Ellis Island processed Europeans; Angel Island restricted Asians. Jane Addams’s Hull House aided assimilation.
Push factors (persecution, poverty) and pull factors (opportunity, freedom) drove the largest migration in U.S. history.
Nativism produced restriction: the Chinese Exclusion Act (1882) and the Gentlemen’s Agreement (1907).
The first federal law to bar a nationality — read who the Chinese Exclusion Act shut out.

sourceItFirst.why: It was the first U.S. law to bar an entire nationality — ask whom it targeted and what precedent it set.

sources.title: Chinese Exclusion Act
sources.author: U.S. Congress
sources.excerpt: ...the coming of Chinese laborers to the United States be, and the same is hereby, suspended... it shall not be lawful for any Chinese laborer to come... to remain within the United States.

sources.title: Twenty Years at Hull-House
sources.author: Jane Addams
sources.excerpt: We early found ourselves spending many hours in efforts to secure... justice for immigrants... whom the state had left unprotected.

slides.assertion: Return to three questions: who benefited, who bore the costs, who decided.

perspectives.prompt: Who gained land, wealth, power, or protection?
perspectives.answer: Employers gaining cheap labor; the growing industrial economy; immigrants who found opportunity and religious freedom.

perspectives.prompt: Who lost land, labor, freedom, or life — and who was silenced?
perspectives.answer: New immigrants facing discrimination, tenement poverty, and hostility; Chinese and Japanese immigrants barred by exclusion laws.

perspectives.prompt: Which people, offices, or courts held the authority?
perspectives.answer: The U.S. Congress (Chinese Exclusion Act, 1882) and the executive branch (Gentlemen’s Agreement, 1907), driven by rising nativism.
